title: SYSK Distraction Playlist: How Pinball Works
summary: A distraction-playlist rerun of Stuff You Should Know on pinball. Josh and Chuck open with banter about Las Vegas and Josh's brother's home game room, then trace pinball history from 19th-century bagatelle tables through Montague Redgrave's spring-loaded ball shooter, the 1930s explosion of features (coin operation, bumpers, tilt, scoring), and the 1947 flipper invention by Gottlieb (Humpty Dumpty). They cover the mid-century bans on pinball in New York (LaGuardia, Pearl Harbor-era raids), the decades-long illegality, Oakland's 2013-era repeal, Roger Sharp's City Council demonstration that saved the game, the 1990s decline and Pinball 2000, Stern's survival and the modern revival, and collector markets. The second half explains how pinball works: playfield, flippers, ball specs, the black box and backglass, electro-mechanical vs. solid-state parts, solenoid plungers, scoring modes like multiball and wizard modes, replays and match, and tilt and slam tilt. The episode ends with listener mail about a doctor's experience with patients who bring in supposed parasites.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about Las Vegas, and Josh mentions his brother's game room with pinball machines and an arcade cabinet.

segments.title: Early pinball and the 1930s innovation boom
segments.summary: The hosts trace pinball to nineteenth-century bagatelle tables, Montague Redgrave's spring-loaded ball shooter, and the 1930s explosion of features like coin operation, bumpers, tilt, and scoring. The Depression made cheap pinball popular, and Chicago became a pinball hub as the number of manufacturers fell from 145 to 14.

segments.title: Flippers and the shift to skill
segments.summary: Before flippers, players could only nudge the machine, so pinball was closer to a game of chance. Flippers arrived in 1947 with Gottlieb's Humpty Dumpty, and early flippers were short and faced the reverse direction until Gottlieb's Spot Bowler in the 1950s set the modern arrangement.

segments.title: Pinball bans and LaGuardia's raids
segments.summary: Pinball was outlawed in many US cities because it was seen as gambling. New York mayor Fiorello LaGuardia banned it, and after Pearl Harbor police raided and destroyed machines, dumping them in the river. From the 1940s to the mid-1970s, playing in many cities meant finding machines behind curtains in pornography shops.

segments.title: Oakland repeal and Roger Sharp's City Council demonstration
segments.summary: Oakland overturned its eighty-year pinball ban. Pinball was also linked to rebellious youth culture, referenced through The Who's Tommy and a Simpsons quote. In New York, Roger Sharp demonstrated at a City Council hearing that pinball was a game of skill, using a Babe Ruth-style called shot up the middle, which helped get the ban repealed.

segments.title: Pinball rankings and the decline of pinball
segments.summary: The hosts list top-ranked players, including Keith Elwin of the USA, Roger Sharp's son Zach Sharp, and Josh Sharp in the top twenty. Pinball enjoyed a golden age in the 1990s, but declined as video games arrived and manufacturers dwindled.

segments.title: Pinball 2000, Stern, and the modern revival
segments.summary: By the 1990s Bally and Williams pulled out, leaving Pinball 2000, a hybrid with video screens and interactive playfield elements that was not well received. Stern became the main manufacturer, and Jersey Jack Pinball and Stern's rehiring led to a modest revival. Home sales are a growing share of Stern's business, and many vintage games are being imported from overseas.

segments.title: Mechanics of pinball: playfield, flippers, and ball
segments.summary: The core parts of pinball are the flippers and the ball, with the playfield tilted about six to seven degrees toward the player. The steel ball is about 1.06 inches in diameter, weighs roughly 2.8 ounces, and can reach about 90 miles per hour. Some games use ceramic Powerballs, which are immune to magnets.

segments.title: Black box, backglass, and electro-mechanical parts
segments.summary: The black box connects the playfield to the backglass and holds the electronics. Solid-state electronics took over scoring and sound in the 1970s, but the playfield mechanics remain electro-mechanical, with about half a mile of wiring. The playfield is wood, and some newer games use LCD or plasma screens.

segments.title: Launching the ball, scoring modes, and replays
segments.summary: Solenoid plungers now launch balls, replacing the earlier manual plunger that could be used to send extra balls. Scoring centers on combination shots and game-within-a-game modes, such as High Roller's poker-based Casino Frenzy and Wizard modes with multiball. Free games come from replay score thresholds or from match, a random-number bonus.

segments.title: Tilt and slam tilt
segments.summary: Tilt prevents players from cheating by moving the machine. A metal ballast swings inside a copper ring, and contact sends a signal to the motherboard. Most games give two warnings before flippers stop and the ball is lost. A slam tilt, from hitting the machine hard, shuts the game down.

segments.title: Listener mail on parasite misdiagnosis
segments.summary: A listener shares a physician's comments about patients who bring in supposed parasites that prove to be lint and hair, and why anti-parasitic medication should not be prescribed without evidence. The episode closes with reminders to contact the show.
